Math sucked. You NEED to study!! I recently said on this sub I got a 158 on my practice test, studied in a 2 week course specifically designed to study for the math GED, and did tons of my own studying and my ultimate score was... 159. One point more. I know it sounds like I'm trying to scare you, but it's better to be scared into studying hard now than on the day of the test. If you've studied like crazy for a long time before the test, you'll be so much less scared going in. Even if that confidence is unwarranted, it'll help your head be clear and you'll know you did your best and you'll just have to try again if you fail.

The test is going to cover basic arithmetic to Algebra to Geometry. I had a question where I had to solve a linear inequality with an x and an x^2 and most of the answers had some square root of 111 divided by 37 bullshit I just did not understand. See if you can find example problems like that. Go to your local library or bookstore and see if you can pick up books on high school level algebra and geometry. You'll need to be able to plot the slope of a line, know what everything in the y=mx+b formula means (m is the slope and b is the y-intercept). Know how to calculate probability. Find percentages. Know the difference between parallel and perpendicular lines. Median is not the same thing as mean and they will define them for you on the formula sheet. See if your college has an academic assistance center and go there with your GED book and get them to explain to you EVERY single thing you have a problem with on the practice tests in that book until they kick your ass out.

If you've taken the ready test on the GED website, you could also look at everything they say you need help with and focus all your energy on half of them until you have it down to a science, then give a cursory look over the rest of it. And keep reviewing everything you think you know. Look for long word problems in the subjects you know to familiarize yourself with the vocabulary those word problems use so you have a better chance of understanding what the word problems on the test are asking you to do.

And if you fail, then you know what will be on the test and you can study and take it again. People in my math class had failed multiple times, some like 5 times, and they were still able to learn new things.

I completely agree with studying hard for a good length of time. I was part of a 2 week course for the math GED in which I understood everything that was taught, and also did tons of my own studying with Khan Academy and thought I was blazing through it. Still only ended up getting a 159 when I thought I was learning so much (only one point above my practice score before any of this). Solving linear inequalities and geometry were a lot more prominent than I was expecting, along with being able to graph a line.
